In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Ghashiyah (The Overwhelming).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has the news of the Overwhelming reached you?﴾ ﴿Faces that Day will be humbled,﴾ ﴿laboring, weary.﴾ ﴿They will burn in a Fire intensely hot,﴾ ﴿made to drink from a boiling spring.﴾ ﴿They will have no food except from thorny plants,﴾ ﴿which neither nourish nor satisfy hunger.﴾

The discussion regarding "hal" (هَلْ) here is like the discussion regarding "hal" in the opening of Surah al-Insan: is it interrogative, or is it in the sense of "qad" (قَدْ, indeed)?

Abu al-Su'ud and others preferred that it is interrogative, for drawing attention, for intensifying the sense of wonder, and for highlighting the importance of this news. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "He had not come to him so that he could inform him of it." The "news of the Overwhelming" is its account, which speaks of it.

As for "al-Ghashiyah" (الغاشِيَةُ), Abu Hayyan said: its original meaning in the language is a calamity that covers people. Scholars differed about what is intended here. It was said: it is the Day of Resurrection. And it was said: it is the Fire. Each speaker supported his view with texts. From the first view is His saying: ﴿On the Day the punishment will envelop them﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 55].

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: The Resurrection was named by this name because whatever surrounds a thing from all its sides covers it, and the Resurrection is like that in several respects:

First: it comes upon creation suddenly, as in His saying: ﴿Are they then secure from the coming upon them of an overwhelming punishment from Allah, or the Hour coming upon them unexpectedly?﴾ [Yusuf: 107].

Second: it covers all people, from the first and the last.

Third: it covers people with terrors and hardships.

(p-509) From their evidence that it is the Fire is His saying: ﴿And the Fire will cover their faces﴾ [Ibrahim: 50].

It was also said: al-Ghashiyah refers to the people of the Fire who "overwhelm" it, meaning they enter it, so al-Ghashiyah is like the crowding (al-Daffah) in the hadith about the sacrificial animals.

Al-Tabari said: "In my view, the preferred opinion is that Allah, exalted is He, stated it in general so that it encompasses all, and therefore it must be taken in its general sense as well."

What appears to be preferred — and Allah knows best — is that it refers to the general Resurrection, not specifically to the Fire; the Fire is among the terrors and calamities of the Resurrection, and this is what the Qur'an supports in this context in several respects, among them:

That after it comes His saying: ﴿Faces that Day﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 2], and "Day" is more fitting to the Resurrection than to the Fire.

Among them: the explicit statement afterward that those whose characteristics are these: ﴿They will burn in a Fire intensely hot﴾, which indicates that the Overwhelming is something other than the intensely hot Fire.

Among them: that the generality concerning the Day of Resurrection includes all creatures, and this is most fitting to the standing place (of judgment), after which Allah saves those who were mindful of Him.

Allah has also explained the counterpart of this category, which indicates that the news intended as an announcement concerns the state of the general standing place.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 88, verse 2:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Faces that Day will be humbled﴾, ﴿labouring, weary﴾, ﴿burning in a scorching Fire﴾ — and so on. They agreed that "that Day" (yawma'idhin) means the Day of Resurrection.

Abu Hayyan said: The tanwin in it is tanwin 'iwad (the tanwin of compensation). It is a tanwin of compensation for a sentence (jumla), but no sentence preceded it that could be the thing the tanwin compensates for; rather, the word al-Ghashiya had preceded it. And al (the definite article) here is a relative (mawsula) attached to the active participle, so it resolves into "the one which overwhelms" (allati ghashiyat), that is, "the calamity which overwhelms." Thus the tanwin is compensation for this sentence into which the word al-Ghashiya resolves, and into the relative pronoun which is allati. This strengthens and supports what we previously put forward, that al-Ghashiya is the Resurrection. (p-510)

﴿Faces that Day will be humbled﴾, meaning: abased. Abu al-Su'ud said: This and what follows came as an answer to a question that arose from the earlier rhetorical interrogation (al-istifham al-tashwiqi), as if it were said on his part, peace and blessings be upon him: "There has not come to me the report of it," so God Most High informed him, and said: "Faces..." etc.

He said: There is no harm in its being indefinite (tankir), because it is in a position of classification (tanwi'), that is, the position of classification is what permitted beginning with an indefinite noun: "faces of such-and-such kind, and faces of such-and-such kind."

And khashi'a ("humbled") is the predicate of the subject; that is, what follows it is among their attributes.

As for His saying: ﴿labouring, weary﴾ — 'amal is well known, and naṣab means fatigue. It has been disputed about the time of these two, 'amal and naṣab: is it something that occurred from them in this world, or is it something that will actually befall them in the Hereafter? And on both interpretations: Those who said it occurred from them in this world — among them are those who said: it is labour and fatigue in invalid acts of worship, like the labour of monks, priests and misguided innovators, which will not benefit them on the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23].

And among them are those who said: they laboured, grew weary and took pleasure in what does not please God, so God dealt with them in the Hereafter with the opposite of their intention. But the weakness of this view is evident, because those in such a state are not counted as labouring and weary, rather as enjoying pleasure and delight.

And those who said it will actually take place from them on the Day of Resurrection agreed that it is labour and fatigue in the Fire, from dragging the chains — we seek refuge in God — and their ascending and descending the valleys and ravines, as in His saying: ﴿I will overwhelm him with a rugged ascent﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 17], and His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter an arduous punishment﴾ [al-Jinn: 17].

Al-Fakhr al-Razi mentioned a threefold division. He said: Either all of that occurs in this world, or all of it in the Hereafter, or part in this world and part in the Hereafter. He did not favour any division except that the view that it is in this world applies to the priests and the like. He said: Because they laboured in worshipping a god whom they described with what he is not characterised by, and whom they had only imagined imaginatively — namely by their saying: ﴿third of three﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 73], and their saying: ﴿Ezra is the son of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30] — so their worship was directed to that imagined entity, not to the true God, glorified is He.

(p-511) And it is not far-fetched to say on this view that whoever among those who do not utter the two testimonies, and acts in ignorance in matters for which ignorance is no excuse, may be feared to fall under this verse, just as one fears it for those who act knowingly but in innovation and error.

What bears witness to the first view is the hadith of the one who prays badly. And the report of Hudhayfah: "He saw a man praying and he was astray in it, so he said to him: For how long have you been praying this prayer? He said: For forty years. He said to him: You have not prayed for forty years, and if you die upon this, you will die upon other than the fitrah of Muhammad ﷺ."

And the hadiths related on this matter are in general terms, such as his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever does an action that is not upon our command, it is rejected" — that is, mardud (rejected).

And the hadith of the Pool: "Some people will be driven away from my Pool, and I will say: My community, my community! It will be said: You do not know what they innovated after you; they changed and altered."

And the like of that which necessitates attentiveness to the soundness of the action and its conformity to what the Prophet ﷺ brought.

And likewise the second category, as in His saying: ﴿Say: Shall we inform you of the greatest losers in deeds? Those whose effort is lost in this world﴾ — the verse [al-Kahf: 103–104].

As for the preferred of the two views regarding the time of ﴿labouring, weary﴾ — whether it is in this world or in the Hereafter — it is the view that it is the Day of Resurrection, which is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and a group, and the evidences for it are from the context itself.

Ibn Taymiyyah has a very excellent discussion in favour of this preference, and I have not come across a view from anyone else stronger than it. We cite its gist for benefit:

He said in al-Majmu' in his tafsir of this surah, after relating the two views: The truth is the second, for several reasons, and he set out seven reasons:

First: On the second view, the adverbial phrase is connected to what follows it, that is: faces on the Day of the Overwhelming, humbled, labouring, weary, roasting. Whereas on the first view it is connected only to His saying: "burning." And His saying "humbled" would be an attribute of "faces," separated from it by a foreign element connected to another attribute. The arrangement would be: faces, humbled, labouring, weary, that Day, burning in a scorching fire — and advancing and postponing is contrary to the original; the original is to keep the speech in its order and arrangement, not to change its arrangement, and advancing and postponing occurs only with an indicator.

Second: God mentioned the faces of the wretched and the faces of the blessed in the surah after this: ﴿Faces that Day will be joyful﴾, ﴿pleased with their striving﴾, ﴿in a lofty garden﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 8–10], that is, on that Day, which is the Day of the Hereafter. So it is necessary that the two categories be parallel, that is, in the time-frame.

Third: The parallel of these two categories is what is mentioned in another place in His saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾, ﴿looking at their Lord﴾, ﴿and faces that Day will be scowling﴾, ﴿expecting that a calamity will be inflicted upon them﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22–25], and in another place in His saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be bright﴾, ﴿laughing, rejoicing﴾, ﴿and faces that Day will have upon them dust﴾, ﴿covered by darkness﴾, ﴿those are the disbelievers, the wicked﴾ [‘Abasa: 38–42]. All of this is a description of faces in the Hereafter.

Fourth: The intended meaning of "faces" is their possessors, because the predominant usage in the Qur'an is describing faces with a mark, as in His saying: ﴿Their mark is on their faces﴾ [al-Fath: 29], and His saying: ﴿You would recognise them by their mark﴾ [Muhammad: 30]. However, the indication of this point for the intended meaning is not clear.

Fifth: That His saying "humbled" and "labouring, weary," if it were made an attribute of them in this world, there would be no blame in this expression; rather it is closer to praise, and its utmost is that it is a shared attribute among His believing servants and His disbelieving servants, and blame is not conveyed by a shared attribute. If a specific group were intended, it would have been said: humbled before idols, for example, labouring for other than God, weary in obedience to Satan. And there is no blame in the Qur'an for this attribute at all, nor any threat upon it. So taking it in this sense departs from the known discourse of the Qur'an. This is among the strongest of the views in meaning and the clearest in indication.

It may also be supported by the fact that among these there may be the common folk, deceived by others, who will be utterly remorseful on the Day of Resurrection for following them, as in His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved will say: Our Lord, show us the two who led us astray from among the jinn and mankind; we will put them beneath our feet so that they may be among the lowest﴾ [Fussilat: 29].

Sixth: And this is also important: if it were made for them in this world, it would be specific to some disbelievers and not others, and would be restricted to the worshippers among them, although non-worshippers among them would be worse in deeds and deserve a harsher punishment.

Seventh: That if this address were made to them in this world, the like of it would repel them from the very principle of worship and devotion from the outset — that is, the Sunnah has come with leaving alone the people of the monasteries and ascetics, without confronting them with killing or fighting, just as it has upheld the adherents of religions in their religions, which indicates respect for the principle of devotion in the general sense, as he pointed out.

I have cited the gist of his words, may God have mercy on him, so that the verse is not taken in other than its preferred sense, nor the context carried to other than what it was brought for. He concluded his words with a subtle remark, saying: Then, if that is restricted to the worship of disbelievers and innovators, while the address contains no restriction, this would be an effort to correct the Addresser by what was not mentioned in the address. End of quotation.

Who is it that grants himself the right to correct the address in the speech of the Lord of the worlds? It is a reminder of the necessity and importance of interpreting the Qur'an by the Qur'an, which the Shaykh — may God's mercy be upon us and upon him — followed in Adwa' al-Bayan in interpreting the Qur'an by the Qur'an.

Another aspect has appeared to me: if this labour were taken as referring to disbelievers and innovators, its plain meaning would be that the punishment befell them as recompense for their labour and fatigue in that worship, while the punishment of disbelievers in general is for abandoning works for God alone, and the punishment of innovators is for the misguidance they innovated. So if what they innovated has no connection with the pillars of Islam or with creed, but is in branches of worship which they devised and which were not in the Sunnah, then even though they laboured and grew weary, there is no reward for them in it, and it cannot be said that they are punished for it, since that mentioned punishment is not the recompense for the labour and fatigue mentioned, with the soundness of creed in tawhid and the performance of what is obligatory in the pillars of Islam. And God Most High knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 88, verse 5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will be given to drink from a spring that is boiling hot.﴾

It has been said: [āniyah means] present (ḥāḍirah). And it has been said: [āniyah means] intensely hot. This latter is what the Qur'an supports in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will go around between it and scalding water, boiling hot.﴾ It is known that ḥamīm (scalding water) is intensely hot. Likewise, interpreting it to mean "present" does not clarify the meaning of the kinds of drink in that spring (p-514) prepared and made ready for them. In the lexicon (al-Mu'jam): "ḥamīm āni" means its heat has reached its limit; the verb is anā (ʾanā), the water being heated "yaʾnī" (yaʾnī, with the nūn kasrah). ʿAbbās said:

Conspicuous, while horses cover its backs, a scalding and boiling [liquid] from the blood of the belly, flowing forth.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 88, verse 6:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They shall have no food except from ḍarīʿ (a thorny plant)﴾

The Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on us and on him, spoke about removing the appearance of contradiction from the verses of the Book by reconciling this verse with the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So no friend will he have here today, nor any food except from ghislīn (a discharge of the people of the Fire)﴾ [al-Haqqah: 35–36]. He explained the correct meaning of ḍarīʿ, what it is, and that it is a plant known to the Arabs, and that it is meant literally, not figuratively.

Fakhr al-Din al-Razi raised a question and its answer, namely: how can ḍarīʿ grow in the Fire? He answered by referring to the question of how the bodies of the disbelievers can remain alive in the Fire, and likewise the snakes and scorpions in the Fire.

Although this is sound from the standpoint of the logic of power, the Qur'an has explicitly stated that the Fire contains the tree of zaqqum, and that it is a trial for the wrongdoers, in His words: ﴿Is that better as a hospitality, or the tree of zaqqum? Indeed, We have made it a trial for the wrongdoers. Indeed, it is a tree that emerges from the root of Hellfire; its shoots are like the heads of devils. Indeed, they will eat from it and fill their bellies with it﴾ [as-Saffat: 62–66]. Thus He affirmed a tree that emerges from the root of Hellfire, and affirmed its necessary consequence, which is its shoots in that hideous form, and affirmed the consequence of that consequence, which is their eating from it until their bellies are filled.

The truth is that this question and its answer were raised by the people of falsehood, but the most that is involved is the negation of the property of burning in the Fire from the plant, and this is not far from the power of the One who created the Fire and gave it that property.

A parallel to this has been found in this world: the fire of Nimrod, which would burn birds in the air when they came near it, and they were unable to approach it so as to throw Ibrahim into it; they placed him in a catapult and hurled him from afar. Yet Allah protected him from it by His words to it: ﴿O fire, be cool and safe for Ibrahim﴾ [al-Anbiya': 69]. Glory be to the One in whose hand is the dominion of all things.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Dafʿ Iyhām al-Iḍṭirāb ʿan Āyāt al-Kitāb):

(p. 442) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surah al-Ghashiyah

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They shall have no food except from ḍarīʿ﴾.

The aspect of reconciling it with His words: ﴿nor any food except from ghislīn﴾ [al-Haqqah: 36], and His words: ﴿Therein is a flowing spring﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 12] has already been mentioned.

The apparent meaning of this verse is that Paradise contains one spring, whereas other verses indicate otherwise, such as His words: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and springs﴾ [al-Hijr: 45].

The answer is what was mentioned earlier in reconciling His words: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and a river﴾ [al-Qamar: 54] with His words: ﴿Therein are rivers of water unaltered﴾ [Muhammad: 15].

So by "al-ʿayn" (spring) is meant "al-ʿuyūn" (springs), as its parallel has been mentioned earlier in Surah "al-Baqarah" and elsewhere.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 88, verse 8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Faces that Day will be joyful﴾ ﴿pleased with their striving﴾ ﴿in a lofty Garden﴾ ﴿where they hear no idle talk﴾ ﴿therein is a flowing spring﴾ ﴿therein are raised couches﴾ ﴿and cups set in place﴾ ﴿and cushions arranged in rows﴾ ﴿and carpets spread out﴾ (p-515) This is the counterpart of the first division in describing the condition of the people of Paradise. He did not connect it with the conjunction "wa" (and), signaling the complete contrast between the two contents. As for "that Day" (yawma'idhin): it is the Day of the Overwhelming (yawm al-ghashiyah) mentioned earlier, and this requires that the Overwhelming encompasses both groups, although its effects vary with the different kinds of people. Accordingly, some of them are overwhelmed by its terror, and some of them are overwhelmed by its bounty. It is, for each of the two groups, complete in what overwhelms them, and it applies to both groups.

It is well known that the word al-ghashiyah (the Overwhelming) is applied to good as it is applied to evil, in the sense of comprehensiveness and complete encompassing. Among its application to good is what came in the hadith: "No people sit in a gathering in which they mention God, exalted is He, except that the angels surround them, mercy covers them, and God mentions them among those who are with Him." Related by Muslim.

The explanation of this and its verification concerning both divisions is as follows:

As for the first of them, which is the Overwhelming with respect to the people of the Fire: the punishment has overwhelmed them sensibly and in meaning, outwardly and inwardly, or [there is] no humility in abasement. This is a psychological aspect, and it is sometimes heavier than the material aspect; some people choose death over it. Then, together with the abasement, there is labor and fatigue, sensibly and physically. And with severe fatigue, ﴿they will burn in a blazing Fire﴾, whereas saying "they will burn in fire" would have sufficed. But following it with the description "blazing" is an addition in displaying their punishment and an addition in the punishment overwhelming them. Then they are given to drink ﴿from a boiling spring﴾: extremely hot. So they are between a blazing fire from outside and scalding water from inside, by which their bellies are melted. Thus it is more complete in encompassing them from all aspects. As for the opposite division, it is complete generality and comprehensive joy, as follows: faces that are joyful, complete in blessing, ﴿you will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾.

This, in its comprehensiveness on the immaterial side, is the counterpart in the first division: instead of "humbled, in abasement," [there is] "joyful, in radiance." ﴿Pleased with their striving﴾: which is their effort in the world, and what they strive to attain or its reward. ﴿In a lofty Garden﴾ instead of labor and toil. ﴿Where they hear no idle talk﴾: a lofty moral rank, in that they hear in it no word of vanity, nor is it fitting for it. This is an honor for them even in the words they hear, as in His saying: (p-516) ﴿They hear therein no idle talk nor sinful speech, only the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25–26].

﴿Therein is a flowing spring﴾

It is well known that these are springs and rivers that flow, as in His saying: ﴿in gardens and springs﴾ [al-Hijr: 45]. Among the necessary features of springs and rivers is the perfection of bliss: trees and fragrant plants, ﴿then rest and provision and a Garden of bliss﴾. In this generality it corresponds to the boiling spring of scalding water for the first division.

﴿Therein are raised couches﴾, and they recline upon them, instead of the labor and misery of the others.

﴿And cups set in place﴾ for completing enjoyment and the perfection of service and luxury. ﴿And cushions arranged in rows﴾: reclining places. ﴿And carpets spread out﴾: spread everywhere. Thus bliss is complete from every side, encompassing what the eye sees, what the ear hears, and what they taste of drink and other things.

Thus the bliss has overwhelmed them, just as the retribution overwhelmed those others. The Overwhelming then means the all-encompassing, and in its generality it applies to both groups; it is linguistically and legally suitable both for those punished with punishment and for those blessed with bliss. And success is from God, exalted is He.

Note.

The repetition of "therein" twice: ﴿therein is a flowing spring﴾ and ﴿therein are raised couches﴾, to indicate the two kinds of the Garden's bliss. The first: springs and recreation. The second: couches and repose.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 88, verse 17:**

Almighty Allah says: ﴿Will they not look at the camel, how it was created?﴾ ﴿And at the sky, how it was raised?﴾ ﴿And at the mountains, how they were set up?﴾ ﴿And at the earth, how it was spread out?﴾ ﴿So remind, for you are only a reminder.﴾

The command to look at these four things directs attention to the great signs they contain of Allah's power and of resurrection, and then to the acknowledgment of Allah's oneness and divinity (al-wahdaniyyah wa'l-uluhiyyah), as a consequence of affirming His lordship (rububiyyah) over all His creation.

As for the camel, it is perhaps the thing most familiar to the Arabs and the closest to their lives: they eat its meat, drink its milk, clothe themselves with its wool and hides, and in their settling and travelling they ride on it. Nothing in the whole world provides this, not horses, not elephants, nor any other animal. Allah directed attention to it along with other things in the context of His favour upon them, in His words: (p-517) ﴿Do they not see that We have created for them, of what Our hands have made, livestock, and they are its owners? And We have subdued them for them, so some of them they ride and some of them they eat. And for them in them are benefits and drinks; will they not then be grateful?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71–73].

Likewise, in particular, in His words: ﴿And the livestock, He created them for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and of them you eat. And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home and when you drive them out to pasture. And they carry your loads to a land you could not reach except with great hardship to yourselves. Indeed your Lord is Kind and Merciful.﴾ [al-Nahl: 5–7].

These are manifold blessings and far-reaching benefits, not found in anything else at all, and each of them is in itself a proof of power.

As for the mountains, they are among the things that fill their eyes at all times and occupy their thoughts constantly, because of their nearness to their lives: in the rain and the pasture in their plains, in the shelter in their caves and shade, and in the awe and majesty of their height and their firmness in place. Allah also directed attention to them in another place, in His words: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting place? And the mountains as pegs?﴾ [al-Naba: 6–7], firm, as He also explained that they are anchors for the earth lest it shake with you, ﴿And the mountains He set firm﴾ ﴿as provision for you and your livestock﴾. Thus they are bound up with their lives and the lives of their livestock, as we have already stated.

As for the sky and its raising: that is, its height in its creation, and without pillars that you can see, and without rifts or splitting over the length of time. It too is a focus of their gaze and the object of their needs in watering their livestock.

It is well known that the creation of the heavens and the earth is among the signs of Allah that point to resurrection, as has been mentioned many times before.

The Shaykh had already explained, at His words: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth…﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164], that they are a sign. As for the earth and how it was spread out, the sign in it is general, as in His words: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ [Ghafir: 57].

His words ﴿how it was spread out﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 20] describe a firm sign, because its body, with the consensus (ijma') of the exegetes that it is spherical, is seen as flat, that is, from the point that lies within the extent of the sight. This indicates its vastness and the immensity of its size, because a spherical body, when it reaches such great size and bulk, its surface nearly appears flat from the point of view of one who looks at it. In all of this there are many signs pointing to Allah's power to resurrect creatures and to bring upon them what covers them in their various states.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, had already drawn attention to this meaning when discussing (p-518) His words: ﴿Say: Look at what is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [Yunus: 101], in Surah Yunus.

**Note.**

The direction of attention here is to the manner (kayfiyyah) of the creation of the camel, the setting up of the mountains, the raising of the sky, and the spreading of the earth. Yet "kayf" refers to the state of a thing, and Allah did not make anyone witness any of these: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Kahf: 51]. So how is the question directed to them to look at a manner they did not witness?!

The answer, and Allah knows best, is this: by reflecting upon the results of the creation of the camel, the setting up of the mountains, and so on, even if they do not know the manner, and are unable to grasp its essence and reality, this is more eloquent in establishing the proof against them. It is like one who stands before a marvellous craft whose secret he does not know, and so he asks himself how it was made. Something similar occurred, namely referring to the effect instead of uncovering the essence and manner, in the request of the Friend (al-Khalil, Ibrahim), upon him and upon our Prophet be blessings and peace, asking his Lord to show him how He gives life to the dead. The answer was that He showed him birds flying after he had slaughtered them with his own hand and cut them up, and placed a portion of them on every mountain. He did not witness the manner and essence and reality of the giving of life, which is the stirring of the soul in them and the return of life to them, because that was not within his capacity. But he witnessed the effects that follow from it: their moving, their flying, and their return to what they were before slaughter. Moreover, al-'Uzayr (Ezra) had a similar situation, though clearer in its explanation: he witnessed the bones while He, glorified is He, raised them and then clothed them with flesh. And Allah knows best.

As for His words after that, ﴿So remind, for you are only a reminder﴾, the coming of this command with the particle "fa" (so) in this place indicates that careful observation and deep reflection may lead its possessor to inference (istidlal) concerning the existence of Allah and His power, as the pre-Islamic believer Qass ibn Sa'idah declared in his well-known sermon: "Dark night, and bright day, and a sky of constellations, and stars that shine, and seas that surge, and mountains set firm, and an earth spread out, and rivers flowing." Here he mentioned the sky, the mountains, and the earth.

And like the saying of Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, the well-known pre-Islamic believer:

I have submitted my face to Him to whom the earth submits, bearing heavy rocks;
He spread it out, and when it stood even He fixed upon it the mountains.

And I have submitted my face to Him to whom the clouds submit, bearing sweet, pure water;
When they are driven to a land, they obey, and pour upon it in abundant showers.

And I have submitted my face to Him to whom the wind submits, turning from state to state.

It was incumbent upon these intelligent people to look carefully and reflect upon what surrounds them in general, and upon those great signs in particular, where they would find what suffices them.

As it has been said:

In everything there is a sign for Him
pointing to the fact that He is One.

So if their thinking does not guide them, and their gaze is not directed, then remind them, for you are only a reminder. This is general, that is, whether by pointing to His power through those created things, or by recitation of the signs of revelation. And knowledge is with Allah, the Most High.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 88, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾ ﴿Then indeed, upon Us is their reckoning﴾

In it is the indication that al-Iyab (the return) is al-Marji' (the going back, the return to a place or source).

ʿUbayd said:

؎Every absent one returns, but the absent one of death does not return

As in His saying: ﴿To Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you about that in which you used to differ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48]. This is in its literal sense, as in the explicit statement of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 55], to the end of the verse, and His saying: ﴿Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you about that in which you used to differ﴾ [al-An'am: 164].

As for His saying: ﴿Then indeed, upon Us is their reckoning﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 26], the use of thumma (then) indicates the distance between their return and the beginning of their reckoning: ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ [al-Hajj: 47].

As for His saying, "Indeed, upon Us," with the preceding of the emphatic particle (inna), the attribution of that to Allah, may He be exalted, and the use of the preposition ʿala (upon), all of this emphasizes that it will certainly happen, and that it will be with the utmost precision, and that it applies to the small and the great, as in His saying: ﴿And whether you disclose what is in your souls or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284].

(p-520) It is clear that ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾ ﴿Then indeed, upon Us is their reckoning﴾ comes after His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So remind, for you are only a reminder﴾ ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾ ﴿except one who turns away and disbelieves﴾ ﴿then Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment﴾; as consolation for the Prophet ﷺ and as a warning to those who turned away and opposed. Then indeed, the reckoning on the Last Day is not specific to these people; rather it is general to all creatures. But attributing it to Allah, may He be exalted, indicates the meanings mentioned above.

We ask Allah for pardon and well-being.
